subtitle: Leading through conflict means checking what people mean and examining the interests and power involved. Together, you can then develop a usable agreement with clear limits.
scope: For leaders, supervisors, and team leads addressing work disagreements across perspectives, roles, and experiences. This course does not assign cultural traits to groups or diagnose an employee’s intercultural development. Informal problem solving does not replace required reporting, investigation, safety, or employment procedures. Cases are practice.
introTranscript: Disagreement can expose an assumption the team needs to examine. It can also become harder when people interpret the same message differently, have unequal authority, or do not share the same access to information. Leaders need to understand the work problem without turning differences into stereotypes. This course follows a practice cross-unit review of a service proposal. You will distinguish observations from interpretations, check meaning, identify underlying interests, compare feasible options, preserve appropriate formal routes, and build a reviewable agreement. The aim is a sound work process, not a promise that every disagreement ends in consensus or that someone must accept harmful conduct to keep the peace.

lessons.statement: Begin with the event rather than a label for the person.

intro.heading: Separate the event from the story about it
intro.body:
People can see the same exchange and give it different meanings. A quick challenge may be interpreted as disrespect; delayed written comments may be interpreted as avoidance. Neither interpretation is established simply because it feels convincing. Start with specific events, then examine the meanings and workplace practices that matter.

In a practice DHS cross-unit review, one lead questions a proposal during the meeting and another sends concerns the following day. The project sponsor calls the first aggressive and the second unwilling to collaborate. The observable events are the questions and the timing of the comments. Possible explanations include preparation, review responsibilities, information access, or a preferred response method.

Do not infer a person’s national, racial, or other cultural group explains the behavior. Invite the person to describe the concern without making the person represent a group. A careful account can still identify unacceptable conduct. Separating event and interpretation strengthens that examination; it does not require treating every explanation as equally supported.

flashcards.back: A specific action or event that can be described without assigning motive or character.
The meaning someone gives an event; it needs to be checked rather than treated as established fact.
A proposed solution or stated demand.
A need, concern, or purpose behind a position.
Unequal authority, opportunity, or consequences that can affect participation in a disagreement.
A defined action, responsibility, timing, and follow-up that can be checked in practice.

items.title: Specific event
items.body: Name the words, action, timing, and relevant work context without exaggerating. In the review case, describe that comments arrived after the meeting rather than saying the colleague never cooperates. A specific account gives the group something to check and avoids turning a single event into a character judgment.

items.title: Meaning to check
items.body: An interpretation may be useful as a concern to explore, but should be identified as uncertain. The sponsor can ask what affected the comment timing and whether the review deadline was clear. The answer may reveal a missed handoff rather than reluctance, or may reveal a real expectation needing clarification.

items.title: Stereotype
items.body: A cultural label skips the person’s actual explanation and can create a new barrier. Do not say a group is naturally indirect, confrontational, or resistant. In the practice case, examine preparation and participation conditions. Address specific conduct through relevant expectations rather than using identity to settle the disagreement.

tabs.label: Character story
tabs.body: A character story can make the disagreement feel settled quickly, but offers little evidence for a work repair. Calling a colleague difficult does not explain which review step failed. Return to the specific event and the expectation before deciding what action is warranted.

tabs.label: Checkable account
tabs.body: A checkable account identifies the event, its effect, and what remains uncertain. It supports a fairer conversation because the person can correct an assumption or add context. It does not remove the leader’s responsibility to address conduct or a missed work obligation.

tabs.label: Group explanation
tabs.body: A group explanation may look like cultural awareness while actually replacing individual understanding with a stereotype. The person need not accept that identity assignment. Examine how the work was organized and ask about meaning without treating identity as a diagnostic explanation.

check.question: What is the most useful starting account?
check.correct: Questions were raised in the meeting and additional comments arrived the next day; the reasons and review expectations need checking.
wrong: The direct speaker is naturally aggressive.
The delayed comments prove unwillingness to collaborate.
The colleagues’ cultural groups explain the disagreement.
check.feedbackCorrect: The account distinguishes observable events from interpretations and leaves room to examine the relevant workplace practices.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Character and group labels treat an explanation as settled without evidence. Delayed comments alone do not establish motive. Describe the specific event, identify the uncertain interpretation, and check the relevant expectation or condition.

items.text: Three questions were asked before the meeting ended.
Written concerns arrived the following morning.
The timing might reflect a missing review deadline.
The speaker intended to undermine the sponsor.
People from that group always avoid disagreement.
That identity explains the person’s confrontational style.

lessons.next: Next: Prepare a question that checks a colleague’s meaning without assigning intent.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: A sponsor explains a disagreement by labeling one colleague aggressive and assigning a cultural trait to the other.
scenario.prompt: What should the leader do first?
options: Use the labels to decide who should stop participating.
Describe the actual exchange and check meaning and workplace practices.
responses: The labels bypass evidence and can create further barriers.
This provides an examinable starting point without excusing unacceptable conduct.
Different interpretations still require evidence; they are not automatically established.

lessons.transfer: Rewrite a practice disagreement as an event, effect, interpretation to check, and relevant question.

move.control: You can separate events from labels and ask a bounded clarification.
move.failure: A convincing story replaces examination of the actual work.

intro.heading: Check meaning and make participation usable
intro.body:
Checking meaning is more than waiting for a turn to respond. Ask about the work concern and summarize your understanding so the other person can correct it. Keep the summary tentative. Curiosity does not require declaring that the person’s intent was good or that the effect was harmless.

In the practice proposal review, the second lead explains that a key appendix was shared only with the senior group. Staff in the implementation unit could not examine the assumptions before the meeting. A follow-up written response was their available way to contribute. The sponsor’s authority to finalize the proposal makes that route consequential.

A leader can repair access to the relevant material and plan a timely response opportunity. Avoid requiring someone to disclose personal history to validate a perspective. If the issue includes a formal complaint or protected information, use the appropriate route and limits. The conversation should improve understanding of the work rather than require the less powerful person to defend a character label.

items.title: Listening for the concern
items.body: Ask what part of the proposal creates a difficulty and how it affects the work. Summarize the point in your own words and invite correction. In the appendix case, the issue may be missing information rather than a disagreement about the team’s purpose. Do not turn the first explanation into a cross-examination.

items.title: Participation conditions
items.body: Consider who had the material and who controls the decision. A late comment from an implementation unit may reflect unequal preparation rather than unwillingness. Repair the handoff and clarify timing before demanding more visible participation. Different work roles need not be assigned cultural meanings to make this condition important.

items.title: Usable route
items.body: A focused written response can complement discussion when it reaches the decision in time. Explain what remains open and who will consider the input. Do not promise anonymity or require a personal identity narrative. The route’s usefulness is tested by whether the concern receives a substantive response.

tabs.label: Defend immediately
tabs.body: An immediate defense can protect the sponsor’s preferred account but may miss a preventable handoff problem. Listen to the concrete concern first. The sponsor can still explain requirements afterward, with a more accurate understanding of what affected the exchange.

tabs.label: Clarify and repair access
tabs.body: Clarification can reveal missing preparation or unequal information. Repairing that condition gives the discussion a better basis. It does not guarantee agreement, but allows options to be examined with relevant evidence rather than assumptions about willingness or style.

tabs.label: Demand a personal story
tabs.body: Demanding a personal story may appear to deepen understanding but makes participation depend on unnecessary disclosure. A staff member can identify a work barrier without representing an identity group. Focus on the concern and the practical conditions needed to examine it.

check.question: What is a useful response to the missing appendix?
check.correct: Clarify its effect, provide appropriate access, and plan timely input that reaches the decision.
wrong: Require staff to explain their cultural background.
Insist the late comments show resistance.
Assume the appendix caused every disagreement.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response addresses the participation condition while keeping conclusions about the whole disagreement appropriately limited.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Identity disclosure and a resistance label do not repair missing information. The appendix also may not explain every concern. Check its effect, repair access, and examine the remaining questions rather than use a new assumption as the answer.

items.text: Ask which assumption the colleague could not verify.
Invite correction of your summary of the concern.
Only senior staff received a key appendix.
The sponsor controls when the decision closes.
Require a personal story before accepting input.
Tell the employee to prove good intent.

lessons.next: Next: Distinguish a preferred solution from the need it is intended to meet.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Implementation staff lacked a key appendix and sent late comments, but the sponsor interprets the timing as resistance.
options: Check the effect of missing information and create a usable opportunity to respond.
Require every person to disclose why public disagreement feels difficult.
responses: Removal conceals the participation barrier rather than examining it.
This addresses a concrete condition and keeps the work question open.
Personal disclosure is not needed to provide an appropriate response route.

lessons.transfer: Plan a clarification question, a preparation change, and a route into the decision.

move.control: You can check understanding and repair participation conditions.
move.failure: A listening invitation leaves the actual access barrier untouched.

lessons.title: Find the interests beneath competing positions
lessons.summary: Distinguish a preferred solution from the need it is intended to meet.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a preferred solution from the need it is intended to meet.
objectives: Distinguish a preferred solution from the need it is intended to meet.
Identify common and different interests in a work disagreement.
Separate negotiable work choices from requirements outside the leader’s authority.
takeaways: A position states a solution; an interest explains its purpose.
Shared interests do not remove every difference.
Clarify authority before promising a compromise.
lessons.statement: Examine what the options must accomplish before choosing one.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Find the interests beneath competing positions
intro.body:
Two people may argue for different solutions while trying to protect related work needs. One says the proposal must be finalized today; another says the review should wait two weeks. Those are positions. Timely submission, reliable assumptions, and feasible implementation are interests that can help the team develop another option.

In the practice review, the sponsor needs a draft for a scheduled discussion, while the implementation unit needs to check an eligibility assumption before it becomes a recommendation. A provisional draft with the unresolved point clearly identified may serve part of both needs. Whether that option is allowed depends on the actual process and decision authority.

Do not describe every requirement as negotiable or ask staff to compromise away a reporting right. Identify fixed obligations, open choices, and questions needing another authorized office. Understanding interests helps the group create better options; it does not authorize the group to waive policy, confidentiality, legal requirements, or another person’s responsibilities.

Identify common and different interests in a work disagreement.
Separate negotiable work choices from requirements outside the leader’s authority.
What should the leader examine?
lessons.keyStatement: Examine what the options must accomplish before choosing one.

items.title: Position and purpose
items.body: Ask what the preferred solution protects. A two-week delay may protect accuracy, while same-day submission may protect access to a planning discussion. Understanding those purposes creates room for alternatives. It does not mean either deadline is automatically valid or that the leader can promise a schedule change.

items.title: Common and different needs
items.body: Name common needs without erasing remaining differences. Both units may want a workable proposal but disagree about how much uncertainty is acceptable. Document the unresolved assumption and who can verify it. A shared purpose is useful when it leads to a specific decision question rather than a request to stop disagreeing.

items.title: Authority and limits
items.body: Check which choices belong to this group. A provisional draft may be feasible, while changing an eligibility rule is outside its authority. Keep formal reporting rights and required processes available. A compromise that depends on hiding an unresolved requirement is not a sound agreement even if everyone signs it.

tabs.label: Split the difference
tabs.body: Splitting the difference is quick but may fail both interests or violate a fixed deadline. Choosing a date halfway between the two positions does not establish that evidence can be checked or that the submission process permits delay. Examine purpose and authority first.

tabs.label: Interest-based option
tabs.body: An interest-based option addresses the needs behind the demands and can reveal a workable third path. It still needs an authority and feasibility check. A provisional draft should identify uncertainty honestly rather than make an unsupported recommendation look settled.

tabs.label: Waive the requirement
tabs.body: Waiving a requirement can make the conflict disappear temporarily while creating a larger work failure. Clarify who has authority and use that route. A team agreement cannot make a reporting right, confidentiality duty, or policy obligation optional.

check.question: Which statement separates a position from an interest?
check.correct: “Wait two weeks” is a proposed solution; verifying the eligibility assumption is a purpose the solution may serve.
wrong: The midpoint between requested dates is always fair.
A shared purpose authorizes the team to waive policy.
check.feedbackCorrect: The distinction supports another feasible option without pretending that all requirements can be negotiated.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Deadlines may reflect real obligations, a midpoint may not meet the needs, and shared purpose does not create authority. Identify what each proposal protects and check which choices the group can actually make.

items.text: Finalize the draft today.
Delay the review for two weeks.
Use a verified eligibility assumption.
Have material ready for the scheduled discussion.
The group cannot change the eligibility rule.
An informal team agreement cannot require complaint withdrawal as a gate to participation or reporting.

lessons.next: Next: Define criteria that connect an option to the work’s purpose and access needs.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: The sponsor wants a draft today and the implementation lead wants two weeks to check an assumption.
options: Which person should win the deadline argument.
The interests, fixed requirements, and feasible options within the group’s authority.
A compromise that suppresses the unresolved assumption.
responses: A winner does not establish a workable process.
This can reveal an honest option meeting relevant needs.
Concealing uncertainty weakens the proposal and follow-through.

lessons.transfer: Map two positions to interests, fixed obligations, and one option requiring an authority check.

move.control: You can clarify interests and decision limits.
move.failure: A compromise hides the requirement that caused the disagreement.

lessons.summary: Define criteria that connect an option to the work’s purpose and access needs.
lessons.objective: Define criteria that connect an option to the work’s purpose and access needs.

takeaways: Use criteria that examine the work rather than rank personalities.
An option can help one need and burden another.

lessons.statement: A workable option needs more than agreement in the room.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Compare options using clear work criteria
intro.body:
After understanding the interests, compare feasible options. Relevant criteria may include accuracy, access, workload, timing, and decision authority. Explain the criteria before selecting the preferred choice. Do not score an employee’s loyalty or communication style as though it were a measure of the option.

In the practice proposal review, the group compares delaying the entire draft, submitting it unchanged, and preparing a provisional draft with the uncertain eligibility point flagged. The third option may meet the planning need while protecting an evidence check, but only if the receiving process accepts a provisional draft and the uncertainty is visible.

Ask who bears the added work and whether that person has the capacity and authority to complete it. Consensus from senior staff does not establish that implementation staff can deliver the plan. A bounded choice can acknowledge a tradeoff, assign the evidence check, and identify when the draft must be revisited. That is stronger than declaring a perfect compromise without examining its conditions.

Compare an option’s benefit, burden, and unresolved condition.
Select a next step with a stated reason and responsibility.
What is the next step?
lessons.keyStatement: A workable option needs more than agreement in the room.

items.title: Criteria
items.body: Choose criteria connected to the decision, such as whether the option preserves accuracy and usable participation. In the provisional-draft case, the receiving process and source-check timing matter. Criteria help people understand the reason for a choice and challenge a missing condition without being labeled uncooperative.

items.title: Burden
items.body: Trace who will do the extra work. A solution that asks implementation staff to verify the assumption overnight may reproduce the original access problem. Examine capacity and responsibilities before treating the option as feasible. A senior group’s approval does not establish that all affected work can actually be completed.

items.title: Reason and uncertainty
items.body: Explain why the option is chosen and what remains unsettled. The provisional draft can identify the assumption, the checking responsibility, and the next decision point. This makes the plan reviewable. Avoid a scoring display that implies a precise or objective answer when the criteria and evidence remain judgment-based.

tabs.label: Unchanged submission
tabs.body: Submitting unchanged meets the immediate schedule but leaves the disputed assumption hidden. It can transfer the problem to later implementation. If a requirement remains uncertain, identify it honestly and use the appropriate authority rather than treat speed as the only criterion.

tabs.label: Complete delay
tabs.body: A complete delay may allow review but can miss a relevant planning opportunity. Examine whether all parts actually require delay and who can authorize it. The option is not automatically wrong, but its tradeoff should be clear rather than framed as resistance to action.

tabs.label: Bounded provisional draft
tabs.body: A provisional draft may preserve a planning opportunity while making uncertainty visible. Its benefit depends on the receiving process and a credible source-check plan. Assign responsibility and review timing instead of allowing a temporary caveat to become a permanent unresolved assumption.

check.question: What makes the provisional-draft option sound enough to consider?
check.correct: The process permits it, uncertainty is visible, and a feasible evidence check has responsibility and timing.
wrong: It receives the highest unexplained numerical score.
The added work can be assigned without a capacity check.
check.feedbackCorrect: The choice is grounded in authority, evidence, and follow-through rather than status or apparent precision.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Preference, an unexplained score, and an unexamined workload do not establish feasibility. Check the process, show the uncertainty, and assign an evidence check that the responsible person can actually carry out.

items.text: The draft accurately identifies what remains unverified.
Affected staff can contribute before the point closes.
An authorized person can submit a provisional draft.
The source-check owner has time and appropriate access.
The sponsor’s favorite option wins without reasons.
A precise-looking score replaces missing evidence.

lessons.next: Next: Distinguish an ordinary work disagreement from a concern requiring a formal route.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Senior staff favor a provisional draft but have not checked whether it is allowed or who can verify the assumption.
options: Finalize it because the senior group agreed.
Check the conditions and compare benefits, burdens, and uncertainty openly.
Assign an overnight check without asking about capacity.
responses: Status and agreement do not establish feasibility.
This makes the choice defensible and reviewable.
The assignment can create an avoidable implementation barrier.

lessons.transfer: Compare three practice options using purpose, access, burden, authority, and a remaining uncertainty.

move.control: You can make criteria, burdens, and conditions visible.
move.failure: A popular compromise conceals unsupported assumptions or unworkable tasks.

takeaways: The substance of a concern determines the required route.
Informal discussion cannot be a mandatory gate to a complaint.
An agreement cannot require accepting harmful conduct.

intro.heading: Keep informal problem solving within its proper boundaries
intro.body:
An ordinary disagreement about a draft can be addressed through a bounded work conversation. A report of discrimination, harassment, threats, or another matter requiring a formal response needs its proper route. The leader should not decide that it is merely a difference in communication style and keep it in an informal discussion.

In a practice variation of the review case, a staff member reports repeated remarks about a protected characteristic. The sponsor proposes a joint meeting and asks the employee to withdraw the report first. That is not a neutral participation condition. The manager’s duties under applicable policy continue, including immediate reporting of allegations through the appropriate agency route.

Do not require a person to confront a colleague, disclose personal experiences, or agree to reconciliation before accessing the relevant process. The consultant can offer guidance and feedback but is not a permission gate. Some work coordination may continue alongside the formal route, with appropriate authority, privacy, and safeguards. Clarify those responsibilities rather than promise that informal agreement settles every issue.

Identify coercion in a proposed informal resolution.
Choose a next step that preserves reporting access and leaders’ duties.
What should happen?
lessons.keyStatement: Problem solving should not close the route that the concern requires.

items.title: Concern substance
items.body: Look at what is being reported rather than the label conflict. The repeated protected-characteristic remarks raise a different responsibility from disagreeing about an appendix. Use the appropriate agency policy and reporting process. An informal conversation cannot substitute for a required report or establish a legal or investigative conclusion.

items.title: Choice and coercion
items.body: A proposal can become coercive when access to a report or work opportunity depends on accepting it. Requiring complaint withdrawal or forced confrontation makes the process a barrier. Keep the person’s options and formal access clear, and do not use teamwork language to pressure acceptance of conduct.

items.title: Parallel responsibilities
items.body: The team may need a safe, workable review process while a formal concern is routed. Coordinate only the responsibilities within your role and share information appropriately. Do not investigate outside assigned agency procedures or authority, promise absolute secrecy, or use the consultant as approval for a report. Assigned investigation duties remain governed by agency procedures and the authorized role. An operational repair is distinct from the formal outcome.

tabs.label: Informal gate
tabs.body: An informal gate can appear efficient while delaying the route the concern requires. A mandatory joint meeting or withdrawal condition increases pressure on the reporter. Clarify access and fulfill relevant duties rather than measure success by whether the complaint disappears.

tabs.label: Appropriate formal route
tabs.body: The formal route places the matter with the proper authority and preserves applicable duties. It does not mean every work conversation must stop. Coordinate necessary work appropriately without deciding findings or conditions outside your role.

tabs.label: Communication-style label
tabs.body: A communication-style label can minimize the substance of a report and assign cultural meaning without evidence. Listen to the specific allegation and use the relevant policy. Curiosity about meaning does not remove the duty to respond to reported conduct.

check.question: How should a manager respond to reported protected-class remarks?
check.correct: Use the appropriate immediate reporting route and preserve access without requiring a joint meeting or withdrawal.
wrong: Require informal resolution before any report.
Call it a cultural style difference and close it.
Ask the consultant to approve whether reporting is permitted.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response keeps required responsibility and access distinct from optional work problem solving.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A forced informal step, a style label, and consultant permission can each block the proper route. The report’s substance requires the relevant policy response; a work conversation cannot remove that responsibility or determine the formal finding.

items.text: Which appendix needs review before drafting?
How should written comments reach the deadline?
An employee reports repeated protected-class remarks.
An employee reports threats following a complaint.
Withdraw the complaint before discussing a repair.
Confront the colleague publicly before contacting HR.

Use the proper route and coordinate necessary work with appropriate boundaries.
Treat the allegation as a personality clash.
responses: The condition blocks access and does not remove policy duties.
This preserves the formal responsibility and keeps operational coordination bounded.
The label minimizes the actual reported conduct.

move.failure: Conflict-resolution language becomes pressure to suppress a concern.

lessons.title: Build an agreement that can be checked and revised
lessons.summary: Write an agreement with action, responsibility, timing, and review.
lessons.objective: Write an agreement with action, responsibility, timing, and review.
objectives: Write an agreement with action, responsibility, timing, and review.
Distinguish an agreement to try a process from proof that trust is restored.
Plan follow-up that keeps unresolved concerns visible and appropriate routes open.
takeaways: Agreement needs a practical path to action.
Trying a repair does not prove restored trust.
Review the work and keep unresolved concerns visible.
lessons.statement: Follow-through determines whether an agreement works in practice.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Build an agreement that can be checked and revised
intro.body:
A useful agreement describes what changes, who is responsible, when it happens, and how the group will check it. It should fit the work and remain within the participants’ authority. A vague promise to communicate better makes later interpretation difficult and can leave the original participation barrier unchanged.

In the practice review, the sponsor shares the appendix before the next discussion, the implementation lead submits focused questions before a stated review point, and the authorized person confirms the eligibility assumption. The group agrees when the provisional draft will be revisited. These actions can be checked without asking staff to rate one another’s motives or reveal personal experiences.

An agreement to try a new process is not proof that trust has been repaired or that every concern is resolved. At follow-up, examine whether the material arrived, questions reached the decision, and unresolved issues have a responsible route. Explain any change to the plan. Keep formal reporting access available and do not make continued participation conditional on declaring satisfaction.

Distinguish an agreement to try a process from proof that trust is restored.
Plan follow-up that keeps unresolved concerns visible and appropriate routes open.
What should the leader report?
lessons.keyStatement: Follow-through determines whether an agreement works in practice.

items.title: Defined action
items.body: Describe a work action rather than a personality goal. In the review case, share the appendix at an agreed preparation point and identify who verifies the assumption. This is clearer than asking everyone to be less difficult. Confirm that the person responsible has the authority and resources to act.

items.title: Review point
items.body: Choose a practical point to examine implementation and effect. Did the questions arrive in time, and did they inform the draft? A completed handoff shows implementation, while a better review outcome needs further evidence. Check both without claiming that a single successful meeting guarantees future agreement.

items.title: Unresolved concern
items.body: Identify what the agreement does not settle and the appropriate next route. A participant can support a workable handoff while still disputing a policy assumption. Keep that distinction visible. Do not require a declaration of restored trust or complaint withdrawal as evidence that the process succeeded.

tabs.label: Vague promise
tabs.body: A vague promise is easy to accept but hard to implement or review. “Communicate better” does not identify the missing appendix, deadline, or review responsibility. Convert the intention into a specific action and a way to check whether the work changed.

tabs.label: Defined trial
tabs.body: A defined trial lets the group learn from a practical change without overstating its certainty. It needs a clear record, responsibility, timing, and review. If it fails, examine the condition and revise appropriately rather than declare the participants unwilling.

tabs.label: Forced closure
tabs.body: Forced closure may produce a positive-looking record while concealing unresolved concerns. Signing an agreement does not establish trust or eliminate formal options. Record the bounded action and remaining question, and keep an appropriate route available.

check.question: What should the review of the new handoff establish?
check.correct: Whether the agreed actions occurred, how they affected the review, and what remains unresolved.
wrong: That everyone now trusts the sponsor.
That no further concerns can be raised.
That signing the plan proves the policy assumption is correct.
check.feedbackCorrect: The review examines the agreement’s use and effect without turning cooperation into proof of trust or factual accuracy.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Trust, silence, and a correct policy assumption cannot be inferred from signing a plan. Check the actions and their effect, explain limits, and keep unresolved questions and appropriate routes visible.

items.text: Name who shares the appendix and when.
Set the point for revisiting the provisional draft.
Questions reached the authorized person before the deadline.
The source check resolved one stated assumption.
Signing proves that everyone trusts one another.
No additional concern may be raised after the meeting.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: The new handoff worked once and the sponsor wants everyone to declare that trust is fully restored.
options: Universal restored trust because the plan was signed.
The specific change, evidence of its use, and remaining questions with follow-up.

responses: A signature and one trial do not establish trust for everyone.
This communicates an accurate bounded result and a practical next step.
A bounded improvement can be described while disagreement remains.

move.control: You can define, review, and revise a work agreement honestly.
move.failure: A practical trial becomes a declaration that all harm or uncertainty is gone.
move.next: Write an agreement with action, owner, timing, evidence, remaining concern, and next review.

jobAid.subtitle: Clarify the problem, understand the interests, compare options, and confirm what will happen next.
remember: A communication difference does not establish a cultural trait or motive.
Agreement must fit the work, authority, and participation conditions.
Informal resolution does not close access to the proper formal route.

sections.heading: Understand the disagreement
items: Describe the event and separate it from assumptions.
Check meaning and listen for the work concern beneath a proposed solution.
Consider who has information, influence, and a practical way to contribute.

sections.heading: Develop a response
items: Identify what can be negotiated and what requires another authority.
Compare options against work needs, access, and responsibilities.
Avoid forcing disclosure, confrontation, or a complaint withdrawal.

sections.heading: Follow through
items: Confirm action, responsibility, timing, and an appropriate record.
Set a review point and explain how a concern can be raised.
Describe what changed and what remains unresolved without declaring universal success.
